Water at the base of the plant, not on the leaves.

Remove dead or yellow leaves so air can move around the plant.
Feed with compost or a balanced fertiliser during the growing season.

Scab
A fungal disease that leaves olive-brown, velvety spots on leaves and dark, corky patches on fruit. It spreads in cool, wet spring weather.

Rake up and bin fallen leaves in autumn, the fungus survives the winter in them.
Prune the tree open so leaves dry quickly after rain.
In wet springs, a sulfur or copper spray at bud break protects new leaves.
When buying new trees, pick scab-resistant varieties.
Black rot
A fungal disease that causes brown leaf spots with purple edges and rots fruit until it shrivels into hard, black mummies.

Pick off and destroy mummified fruit and spotted leaves.
Prune out dead or damaged wood.
Keep the plant open and airy so it dries fast after rain.
In bad years, a protective fungicide from early in the season can help.
Cedar apple rust
A fungus that needs both apple trees and nearby juniper or cedar trees to complete its life. It makes bright yellow-orange spots on apple leaves.

In spring, look for orange, jelly-like growths on nearby junipers and cut them off.
Remove badly spotted leaves.
If junipers grow close by, plant rust-resistant apple varieties.
A fungicide from the pink bud stage protects leaves in high-risk areas.
Powdery mildew
A fungus that covers leaves with a white, flour-like powder. It loves warm days, cool nights and crowded plants, and slowly weakens the plant.

Remove the worst leaves and throw them away, not in the compost.
Give plants more space and sun so air moves freely.
Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves.
Spray with diluted milk (1 part milk to 9 parts water), potassium bicarbonate, sulfur or neem oil every 7 to 10 days.
Gray leaf spot
A fungal disease that makes long, narrow, gray-tan patches between the leaf veins. It is worst in humid weather and where corn grows in the same spot every year.

Do not plant corn in the same bed next year.
Clear away old corn stalks after harvest.
Choose resistant varieties.
Space plants so leaves dry quickly.
Rust
A fungus that makes small, raised, rusty orange-brown bumps. If you rub one, the powder comes off on your finger.

Remove and bin infected leaves early.
Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
Do not work among the plants when they are wet, it spreads the spores.
Rotate crops and plant resistant varieties next season. Sulfur sprays can slow it down.
Leaf blight
A fungal disease that causes large, long, gray-green or tan patches that dry out the leaves.

Remove and destroy infected leaves and old plant debris.
Rotate crops for at least one year.
Water the soil, not the leaves, early in the day.
Give plants room to dry quickly and choose resistant varieties.
Esca (black measles)
A wood disease of grapevines. Leaves get yellow or red stripes between the veins, like tiger stripes, and berries can show small dark spots.

Mark affected vines and prune them last, in dry weather.
Cut out dead wood well below the damage and remove it.
Seal large pruning cuts.
Keep vines well fed and watered. Badly affected vines may need replacing.
Leaf spot
Fungal or bacterial spots that start small and grow into brown or dark patches, sometimes with a yellow ring. Leaves can turn yellow and drop.

Pick off spotted leaves and throw them away.
Water at the base, early in the day.
Space and prune plants so air moves through.
A copper spray can slow the spread. Clean up plant debris at the end of the season.
Citrus greening
A serious bacterial disease (huanglongbing) spread by a tiny insect, the Asian citrus psyllid. Leaves get blotchy, uneven yellow patches and fruit stays small, lopsided and bitter. There is no cure.

Contact your local agriculture office, in many places this disease must be reported.
Control psyllids on new shoots with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil.
Infected trees usually have to be removed so they do not infect others.
Buy only certified disease-free citrus plants.
Bacterial spot
A bacterial disease that makes small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and sometimes fruit. It spreads fast in warm, wet weather and with splashing water.

Remove spotted leaves and do not compost them.
Water the soil, not the leaves, and avoid sprinklers.
Do not handle plants when they are wet.
Copper spray can slow it down. Next season, use clean seed and rotate crops.
Early blight
A fungus that makes brown spots with rings, like a target, usually on the oldest, lowest leaves first. The leaves then turn yellow and drop.

Remove the lower spotted leaves.
Mulch the soil so spores do not splash up onto the leaves.
Water at the base and keep the leaves dry.
Rotate crops for 2 to 3 years. Copper sprays can protect new growth.
Late blight
A fast-moving disease, the one behind the Irish potato famine. Large, greasy, dark patches appear on leaves, often with white fuzz underneath in damp weather. It can kill a plant within days.

Act quickly: pull out infected plants, bag them and put them in the bin. Do not compost.
Check nearby tomato and potato plants every day.
Keep leaves dry and give plants space.
Copper sprays can protect healthy plants. Do not replant potatoes from infected plants.
Leaf scorch
A fungus that makes many small purple spots that join together until the leaf looks burnt and dries up.

Remove old, infected leaves after harvest.
Keep the bed weeded and the plants not too crowded.
Water the soil in the morning.
Replant with healthy, resistant plants every few years.
Leaf mold
A fungus of humid places such as greenhouses. Pale yellow spots appear on top of the leaf, with olive-green or brown fuzz underneath.

Lower the humidity: open vents or doors and space plants out.
Remove the affected leaves.
Water the soil, not the leaves.
Grow resistant varieties if it keeps coming back.
Septoria leaf spot
A fungus that makes many small, round spots with dark edges and pale gray centers, starting on the lower leaves.

Remove spotted lower leaves as soon as you see them.
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto the leaves.
Water at the base and stake plants off the ground.
Clean up plant debris at the end of the season and rotate crops.
Spider mites
Tiny sap-sucking mites that live under the leaves. Leaves get fine yellow speckles and you may see thin webbing. They love hot, dry weather.

Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water every few days.
Raise the humidity around the plant.
Use insecticidal soap or neem oil, covering the undersides of the leaves.
Remove badly infested leaves.
Target spot
A fungus that makes brown spots with light rings, a lot like early blight. It can also mark the fruit.

Remove infected leaves and plant debris.
Prune the lower leaves for better airflow.
Water at the base, early in the day.
Rotate crops. A protective fungicide can help in wet seasons.
Yellow leaf curl virus
A virus spread by whiteflies. Leaves curl upward, stay small and turn yellow at the edges, and the plant stops making fruit. There is no cure.

Pull out and bag infected plants so whiteflies cannot spread the virus.
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps, insecticidal soap or neem oil.
Cover young plants with fine insect netting.
Plant resistant varieties next time.
Mosaic virus
A virus that makes a patchy light and dark green or yellow pattern on the leaves, which may also curl or pucker. It spreads by touch, tools and sap-sucking insects. There is no cure.

Remove infected plants and put them in the bin. Do not compost.
Wash your hands and tools after touching plants.
Control aphids and other sap-sucking insects.
Use resistant varieties and virus-free seed.
Cercospora leaf spot
A fungus that makes round spots with light gray centers and dark edges, like a frog eye. Badly spotted leaves fall early.

Remove spotted and fallen leaves.
Water the soil and avoid wetting the leaves.
Do not crowd the plants.
Rotate crops. A copper spray can slow the spread.
Mites and thrips
Tiny pests feeding on the leaves. Leaves curl, crinkle, get silvery or bronze patches and stay small.

Check under the leaves and on new shoots, a magnifier helps.
Spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5 to 7 days.
Use blue or yellow sticky traps to catch thrips.
Remove badly damaged shoots and keep weeds down.
Nutrient deficiency
The plant is short of food. Yellowing between the veins, pale new leaves or purple tints usually mean it is missing nitrogen, magnesium, iron or another nutrient.

Feed with a balanced fertiliser or well-rotted compost.
For yellowing between the veins of old leaves, try Epsom salt (magnesium), 1 tablespoon in 4 litres of water.
Make sure the soil is not waterlogged or too alkaline, both stop roots taking up food.
A simple soil test kit tells you exactly what is missing.
Iris yellow spot virus
A virus spread by onion thrips. It makes straw-colored, diamond-shaped patches on the leaves and can make the bulbs smaller.

Control thrips with insecticidal soap, neem oil and sticky traps.
Remove and destroy badly affected plants.
Keep weeds down, they shelter thrips.
Rotate crops and do not plant onions next to last season's onion bed.
Purple blotch
A fungus that makes small white spots that grow into purple-brown blotches with yellow edges, mostly in warm, humid weather.

Remove infected leaves and old onion debris.
Space plants and water in the morning.
Do not overdo nitrogen fertiliser.
Rotate crops. A copper spray can protect the leaves.
Insect damage
Insects are chewing or sucking the leaves. You may see holes, ragged edges, sticky residue or the insects themselves.

Look under the leaves and pick off any caterpillars, beetles or eggs.
Spray with a strong jet of water, insecticidal soap or neem oil.
Plant flowers nearby to attract helpful insects like ladybirds.
Use fine netting to keep pests off young plants.
White mold
A fungus that makes soft, water-soaked patches covered in white, cotton-like growth, often with hard black specks inside.

Carefully remove infected plants and the soil right around them.
Give plants space and do not overwater.
Water in the morning so plants dry before night.
For a few years, grow crops like corn or onion in that spot instead.
Wilt
The plant droops even when the soil is moist. Often a fungus or bacteria is blocking the stems that carry water, or the roots are damaged.

Check the soil first: water if it is dry, improve drainage if it is soggy.
Cut a stem open: brown streaks inside point to a wilt disease.
Remove badly wilted plants and do not plant the same kind there for a few years.
Use resistant varieties or grafted plants next time.
Bacterial wilt
A bacterial disease that causes soft, yellow, water-soaked patches and drooping. On money plant the leaves turn yellow and the stems can rot.

Cut off infected leaves and stems with clean scissors.
Let the soil dry out between waterings and never leave the pot standing in water.
If the roots smell bad or look brown and mushy, repot in fresh, well-draining mix.
If the plant is badly hit, start a new one from healthy cuttings.
Too much manganese
There is too much manganese in the soil, often because it is acidic, waterlogged or over-fertilised. Leaves get brown speckles and yellow edges.

Stop fertilising for a few weeks.
Flush the pot with plenty of clean water and let it drain fully.
If it does not improve, repot into fresh potting mix.
From now on, use a balanced fertiliser at half strength.
Cordana leaf spot
A fungus that makes oval, pale brown spots with a yellow ring, usually along the edges of the leaf.

Cut off badly spotted leaves and take them away.
Improve drainage and do not crowd the plants.
Feed with a potassium-rich fertiliser to make the plant stronger.
A copper spray can protect new leaves in wet weather.
Pestalotiopsis leaf spot
A fungus that makes gray to brown spots with dark borders, often on leaves that are weak or damaged.

Remove affected leaves.
Avoid damaging the leaves and keep the plant well watered and fed.
Improve the airflow around the plant.
A copper spray can protect new leaves.
Sigatoka
A fungal disease that makes yellow streaks which turn into brown or black dead patches, killing large parts of the leaf.

Cut off and remove heavily affected leaves.
Keep space between plants and remove extra suckers.
Good drainage and balanced feeding keep plants stronger.
In bad years, a regular fungicide or mineral oil spray may be needed.
Angular leaf spot
A fungus that makes brown spots with straight, angular edges, boxed in by the leaf veins.

Remove infected leaves and old bean plants.
Use clean seed from a trusted source.
Do not touch the plants when they are wet.
Grow something other than beans in that bed for 2 years.
Leaf curl
Usually a virus spread by whiteflies. Leaves curl downward, crinkle and turn thick and leathery, and the plant stops growing.

Remove badly affected plants.
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps, neem oil or insecticidal soap.
Keep weeds down around the plant.
Start new plants from healthy seedlings.
Mealybugs
Small, white, cotton-like insects that suck sap. They leave sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, and the leaves can curl and turn yellow.

Wipe them off with a cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol.
Spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil every week until they are gone.
Control ants, they protect mealybugs.
Prune off heavily infested parts.
Ringspot virus
A virus spread by aphids. Leaves get yellow mottling and can become narrow and twisted, and the fruit shows dark rings. There is no cure.

Remove and destroy infected plants quickly.
Control aphids with insecticidal soap or neem oil.
Do not grow cucumbers or melons nearby, they can carry the virus.
Grow tolerant varieties and start with healthy seedlings.
Anthracnose
A fungus that makes sunken, water-soaked spots that turn tan or brown with darker edges.

Remove and bin infected leaves.
Water the soil, not the leaves.
Rotate crops and clear plant debris after harvest.
Use disease-free seed.
Downy mildew
A disease that makes yellow patches on top of the leaf with gray or purple fuzz underneath, especially in cool, damp weather.

Remove infected leaves.
Space plants out to improve airflow.
Water at the base, in the morning.
A copper spray can protect healthy leaves. Choose resistant varieties.
Shot hole
A fungal or bacterial disease that makes small reddish spots which fall out, so the leaf looks like it is full of tiny holes.

Rake up and destroy fallen leaves.
Prune out infected twigs in dry weather.
Avoid watering over the leaves.
A copper spray in autumn, as the leaves fall, can reduce next year's infection.
Alternaria leaf spot
A fungus that makes small, round, brown spots, sometimes with darker rings. It can make leaves drop early in summer.

Remove fallen leaves.
Prune for good airflow.
Keep the tree well watered and fed to reduce stress.
A protective fungicide may help in warm, wet seasons.
Aphids
Small, soft insects that cluster under the leaves and on new shoots, sucking sap. The leaves curl and get sticky.

Blast them off with a jet of water.
Spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil.
Welcome ladybirds and lacewings, they eat aphids.
Do not overdo nitrogen fertiliser, it makes the soft growth aphids love.
Leaf blotch
A fungus that makes small yellowish spots which join into large brown blotches on both sides of the leaf.

Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Plant only healthy rhizomes.
Avoid waterlogged soil and space the plants out.
Rotate crops. A copper spray can slow it down.
Black spot
The most common rose disease. A fungus makes round black spots with feathery edges, then the leaves turn yellow and fall.

Pick off spotted leaves and clear away fallen ones.
Water at the base in the morning, never on the leaves.
Prune for an open center with good airflow.
Spray neem oil, sulfur or a rose fungicide, and grow resistant varieties.
Dry leaf
The leaf is drying out. Common causes are too little water, heat or wind, too much fertiliser, or root damage.

Water deeply once or twice a week instead of a little every day.
Mulch around the base to keep the soil moist and cool.
Check the roots and drainage.
Remove dead leaves and stems.
